chapters.title: The 20-Hour Week
chapters.tease: Twenty hours a week is not an apology. It is the design spec that forced one engineer to find leverage.

chapters.title: Poms and the Overnight Shift
chapters.tease: Why 24-minute blocks, not 25, and why the real work now happens while the engineer is asleep.

chapters.title: One Front Door
chapters.tease: A drawer full of good tools was costing him his sharpest minutes every morning. The fix was one door.

chapters.title: Skills as an OS, Not a Toolbox
chapters.tease: A pile of skills grown by accretion had overlaps and gaps. Five pillars and an old consulting rule fixed it.

chapters.title: The Bias Toward Shipping
chapters.tease: When in doubt, ship, but only because the escape hatches were built first. This is speed as a dividend, not courage.

chapters.title: The Tooling I Started With
chapters.tease: A gateway, a command line and a chat bot. Three early tool choices quietly dictated an entire architecture.

chapters.title: Brand Tokens as Constraints
chapters.tease: A chapter about colour that is really about why deciding the blue once, forever, makes an engineer faster.

chapters.title: Three Tenants, One Machine
chapters.tease: The day a fourth client became almost free was the day the database, not good intentions, enforced the walls.

chapters.title: What "Done" Actually Means
chapters.tease: It works when I run it is a definition of done with a hole big enough to drive a failed demo through.

chapters.title: The Morning Merge
chapters.tease: When the machine can produce ten versions overnight, the scarce act in the morning is rejection, not production.

chapters.title: The Ladder
chapters.tease: Three rungs, and most of the trouble came from standing on the wrong one, usually a rung too high.

chapters.title: Test Once, Expose Twice
chapters.tease: The single most useful structural habit he has is almost embarrassingly simple: one brain, many dumb doors.

chapters.title: The Dumb Frontend
chapters.tease: He wants his frontend as stupid as possible, and means it as the highest compliment.

chapters.title: Streaming Is the Interface
chapters.tease: Thirty seconds of a spinner is indistinguishable from a hang. Streaming is not an optimisation, it is the interface.

chapters.title: Route by Cost, Not by Loyalty
chapters.tease: Sending a trivial classification to your most expensive model is like taking a taxi to check the mailbox.

chapters.title: Adapters, or How to Change Your Mind Later
chapters.tease: The first and most important escape hatch: a thin agreed shape that lets you swap the supplier without the consumer noticing.

chapters.title: The Mock/Live Switch
chapters.tease: One flag decides whether the system is real or pretending. Build it wrong and mock mode becomes a second, broken product.

chapters.title: Leave a Trace
chapters.tease: A run that succeeds silently and one that fails silently look identical. The trace is what buys back your absence.

chapters.title: Know What Every Run Costs
chapters.tease: Interactive calls and headless calls can bill from different pools at different rates. He found out one week before it would have hurt.

chapters.title: When a Rung Runs Out
chapters.tease: Awkward code is a refactoring problem. Fragile workarounds are a ceiling. Knowing the difference is the whole skill.

chapters.title: An Agent Behind a Server
chapters.tease: An agent nobody is watching, called like a function, is the engine room of everything. One you talk to is a tool; a hundred you orchestrate is a factory.

chapters.title: The Subprocess Pattern
chapters.tease: He runs the same command-line tool a developer would use, but his server spawns it and reads the stream. Every upgrade arrives free.

chapters.title: The Stream in Practice
chapters.tease: Three hops carry a stream from subprocess to pixels, and one buffering link anywhere silently turns the whole thing back into a spinner.

chapters.title: The Environment Trap
chapters.tease: The code was perfect and the system still billed the wrong account, because of one invisible variable it was born with.

chapters.title: The Credit-Pool Split
chapters.tease: He assumed a run was a run, billed from one bucket. Then he learned headless and interactive usage drew from separate pools.

chapters.title: The Missing Middle: Session Resume
chapters.tease: A server restart at minute forty of a 45-minute run throws away thirty-nine minutes of thinking, unless the run can resume.

chapters.title: Parallel Runs
chapters.tease: A hundred parallel runs is not one run done many times. It is a different animal with its own bottlenecks and its own storms.

chapters.title: The Approval Gate
chapters.tease: The machine runs at full speed everywhere except the one place a human must say yes. Put that place exactly where irreversibility begins.

chapters.title: Failure Handling & Retries
chapters.tease: Retrying a request that was never going to succeed is one of the most expensive habits in agentic systems. First, name the shape of the failure.

chapters.title: The Orchestrator
chapters.tease: The thin, unglamorous layer that decides what runs when, with three states and no opinions, is what makes overnight a job description rather than a wish.

chapters.title: Ledgers That Compound Into Something
chapters.tease: A badly shaped ledger is worse than none: it gives you confident numbers that cannot answer a single real question.

chapters.title: The ToS Line
chapters.tease: The terms of service are the list of things that get your account shut off when someone finally looks. He turned down a client over it, and was right.

chapters.title: Subscription vs API
chapters.tease: Subscription for serious work and API for experiments: that assumption is exactly backwards, and the arithmetic says why.

chapters.title: Pricing a PoC
chapters.tease: The price of the first proof of concept is the most consequential number in the whole relationship. Too cheap and nobody shows up to the reviews.

chapters.title: When Overnight Throughput Actually Pays
chapters.tease: Automation has a fixed setup cost. Below a certain number of repeats, it is a loss dressed up as progress.

chapters.title: Unit Economics of Tokens
chapters.tease: Tokens times rate is always wrong, and always wrong in the same direction. The honest cost is one and a half to two times that.

chapters.title: The Discount Trap
chapters.tease: The cheap model that needs three attempts is not cheap. Buy the outcome, not the token.

chapters.title: Fixed-Price vs T&M
chapters.tease: Fixed price means you eat the surprises. Time and materials means the client does. In AI work, the meter runs under both of you.

chapters.title: The Client's Meter
chapters.tease: His technical work was clean and his bill was reasonable. Then the client sent a screenshot of their own provider invoice.

chapters.title: Month-End Reconciliation
chapters.tease: Twenty minutes a month matching ledger to invoice is the most reliable way he has of learning what changed underneath him.

chapters.title: MECE in Practice
chapters.tease: MECE is not a one-off audit. It is a gardening job, and the empty row on the grid tells you what to build next.

chapters.title: Intake-First Pipelines
chapters.tease: Every real pipeline he has built starts with intake, because the messy world has to be contained in exactly one place.

chapters.title: The Adapter Interface, Revisited
chapters.tease: A skill that hard-codes its providers ages badly, and skills live long enough for ageing badly to hurt. Draw the adapter before you need it.

chapters.title: Swappable Data Sources
chapters.tease: Data sources are the dependency most likely to change against your will. Design the interface for what your logic wants, never for what any source exposes.

chapters.title: GitHub as Source of Truth
chapters.tease: When the truth is scattered across laptops, screenshots and chat messages, the truth is nowhere. Every skill lives in Git, on GitHub.

chapters.title: The Skill Scaffold
chapters.tease: The scaffold is boring, obvious and non-negotiable, and that is exactly why thirty skills can compose.

chapters.title: Shared Idioms
chapters.tease: Four idioms turn a pile of scripts into a language, and the only way to keep them consistent is to put them in code.

chapters.title: Deprecating a Skill
chapters.tease: Retiring your own work feels ungrateful. Not retiring it turns a lean suite into a museum.

chapters.title: Skill Telemetry
chapters.tease: You think the skill is useful and succeeds most of the time. Those are opinions until five boring numbers arrive every Monday.

chapters.title: When a Skill Wants to Be a Service
chapters.tease: Most skills should stay skills forever. Graduating one to a service is a one-way door that it has to earn.

chapters.title: Discovery to Roster
chapters.tease: Three conversations decide whether a stranger becomes a roster client or a polite non-fit. Delivery is easy compared to choosing whom to deliver to.

chapters.title: Fusion as a Forcing Function
chapters.tease: Ambition times constraint equals clarity. The engagements that terrify him are the ones that produce his best work.

chapters.title: The MOCK Badge
chapters.tease: A well-crafted mock is more convincing than you think, and the badge is the only thing keeping plausibility from becoming deception.

chapters.title: Human-in-the-Loop as the Billable Moment
chapters.tease: The client is not paying for the hundred drafts the machine made. They are paying for the twenty that survived his review.

chapters.title: Converting a PoC
chapters.tease: A successful proof of concept that ends without a next-step conversation usually ends full stop. Open it before the final deliverable lands.

chapters.title: The First-30-Days Spec
chapters.tease: Verbal agreements about scope are misremembered within weeks. A written first-30-days spec is the cheapest way to compress ambiguity.

chapters.title: The Trust Ladder
chapters.tease: Treat a proof-of-concept buyer like a trusted advisor and your strategic advice sounds like arrogance. Read the rung first.

chapters.title: Scope Drift
chapters.tease: Every engagement drifts. The failure is not the drift, it is four months later when both sides have forgotten the original scope.

facts.label: AI-specific trap
facts.value: The AI can just do it

chapters.title: The "One More Thing" Test
chapters.tease: One thirty-second question at the end of every meeting has saved more engagements than any big discipline in the book.

chapters.title: Reference Clients
chapters.tease: A dozen genuine reference clients is a marketing engine you do not have to maintain, because they maintain it for you.

chapters.title: The Scraper I Refused
chapters.tease: A two-week job with a healthy fee, and he said no. Eight months later, the person who said yes lost their account.

chapters.title: The Billing Cliff I Caught a Week Out
chapters.tease: A paragraph buried in release notes would have raised his headless costs by forty percent. He caught it with a week to spare.

chapters.title: The Charity Kick-Off
chapters.tease: A tenth of the budget, a sixth of the time, and the charity ended up more delighted than most well-funded clients.

chapters.title: The Visual OS I Cut Down to Three Deltas
chapters.tease: Twenty pages describing a visual agentic operating system. What shipped six weeks later was three specific changes, and they all moved the numbers.

chapters.title: The 3am Incident
chapters.tease: At 3am on a Wednesday the phone went. Ninety minutes in pyjamas, a five-minute fix, and the most useful client conversation of the year.

chapters.title: The Model Regression
chapters.tease: Nothing changed on his side, and a skill's success rate slid from ninety-seven to eighty-two percent in three weeks. The model had moved.

chapters.title: The Leaked Prompt
chapters.tease: A carefully engineered prompt ended up screenshotted on social media with ten thousand views. The moat turned out to be a curb.

chapters.title: The Demo That Saved the Deal
chapters.tease: Three vendors, a Friday decision, and by Wednesday the pitch was slipping. A two-minute unplanned live demo turned the room.

chapters.title: The Client Who Left
chapters.tease: The client left in year two, and the honest read was that the relationship had privately ended months earlier. The reviews had stopped in month five.

chapters.title: The Deal I Said No To
chapters.tease: The largest fee he ever turned down came with one condition: exclusivity. The refusal became a better engagement.

chapters.title: On Obsidian
chapters.tease: If the app vanished tomorrow he would open the folder in any editor and carry on. That is the whole case for local-first notes.

chapters.title: Against Heavy LMS Platforms
chapters.tease: The features that make a learning platform impressive to buy are the ones that make it worse to use.

chapters.title: Decoration vs Restraint
chapters.tease: AI made decoration cheap. The right response is more restraint, because the reader's attention was always the expensive part.

chapters.title: Against Ad-Hoc Invocation
chapters.tease: A year of chatting his way through problems produced thousands of transcripts and zero compounding. Then he built the front door.

chapters.title: Don't Polish the Mock
chapters.tease: Ship the ugliest, most obviously fake mock that still shows the shape. The ugliness is the point.

chapters.title: Frameworks as Taste
chapters.tease: Five pillars because that is what his work looked like. Yours might have six. The frameworks in this book are taste, not law.

chapters.title: The Notebook Problem
chapters.tease: It worked for me and it fails for you, and both of you are telling the truth. That is the notebook problem.

chapters.title: The "AI-Native" Label
chapters.tease: When every startup, consultancy and roadmap is AI-native, the label distinguishes nothing. Ask what the model actually does.

chapters.title: On Certifications
chapters.tease: A certificate says you knew what experts thought mattered on some cut-off date. In a field this fast, that date has already passed.

chapters.title: What the Influencers Get Wrong
chapters.tease: The demo genuinely worked. The product version might never work at all. Five ways influencer advice misleads, and none of them malicious.

chapters.title: Checking Product Facts
chapters.tease: The model can write confident, plausible sentences about what your product does, and be simply wrong. Five boring minutes catches it.

chapters.title: Esbuild-Clean Artifacts
chapters.tease: If the linter complains, it is not done. A quality bar borrowed from a JavaScript bundler, applied to everything.

chapters.title: Structured Artifacts Close the Loop
chapters.tease: Prose can be looked at. A structured artifact can be checked, compared and audited. Only one of those closes the verification loop.

chapters.title: Diagrams Without Mermaid Slop
chapters.tease: Every auto-generated diagram looks the same, and sameness is the tell that nobody made a design decision. Hand-shaped SVG is the cure.

chapters.title: Type Safety at the Seams
chapters.tease: Seams are where errors accumulate, because both sides assume what is on the other side. A type at the seam turns assumption into contract.

chapters.title: The Review Pass
chapters.tease: Four reads, each asking one question, spaced hours apart. Fifteen to thirty minutes that reliably turns adequate work into thoughtful work.

chapters.title: Property Tests for Prompts
chapters.tease: The prompt passed on ten examples and broke on the eleventh. Property tests check the class of inputs, not the lucky few.

chapters.title: Shipping a Source of Truth
chapters.tease: A database and a cache meant to agree, and they do not. Which is right? Usually neither. That is why you name one source of truth.

chapters.title: The Tone Check
chapters.tease: Clients never say the tone was off. They just come away trusting you slightly less. Read it aloud and listen for the slips.

chapters.title: Red-Teaming Your Own Output
chapters.tease: Not will it go wrong, but how could it go wrong. Attacking your own work is uncomfortable, and cheaper than a client doing it.

chapters.title: Overnight Compounding as Leverage
chapters.tease: Twenty active hours and a hundred-plus passive ones. The ratio is one to five, and it only compounds if every discipline in the book is present.

chapters.title: The Crontab Punchline
chapters.tease: Most of his career has quietly become a Unix crontab. Not a metaphor. An actual crontab, on an actual server.

chapters.title: Delegating to Your Own Machine
chapters.tease: The laptop stops being a tool you use and becomes a colleague you delegate to. Trust it exactly as far as the safety net reaches.

chapters.title: What's Left for the Human
chapters.tease: If the machine does the mechanical work, what is left? Five things, more concentrated and more tiring than eighty diluted hours ever were.

chapters.title: When to Teach the Machine
chapters.tease: Automate too early and you bake in wrong assumptions. Wait too long and you pay the manual tax forever. The signal is a feeling.

chapters.title: Succession
chapters.tease: What happens to the system when he is not the one running it? Not morbid, just a fragility worth designing against.

chapters.title: The Retiring Skill
chapters.tease: When he finally retired his oldest skill, he discovered he could not fully explain why it worked. The retirement note fixed more than the skill.

chapters.title: The Year-Over-Year Audit
chapters.tease: Month to month the practice looks stable. Over a year, half the roster has turned over and the skill mix has quietly reshaped.

chapters.title: The Exit Interview With Your Own System
chapters.tease: He imagined leaving his own practice and being interviewed on the way out. What he would have to say out loud was what was not written down.

chapters.title: What Comes Next
chapters.tease: One hundred chapters in: not what comes next for the industry, but what the reader should actually do on Monday.
